subject: Climate & Environment
title: Plastic and Marine Wildlife
description: A fast breakdown of Plastic and Marine Wildlife for builders.

hook.text: Over 100,000 marine mammals die from plastic entanglement or ingestion every year.

buildup.text: Sea turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish. Seabirds feed bottle caps to their chicks.

discovery.text: 90% of all seabirds have plastic in their stomachs. In the 1960s, it was less than 5%.

twist.text: Whales have been found dead with over 40 kilograms of plastic in their digestive systems.

climax.text: Plastic doesn't just kill directly. Toxins on its surface enter the food chain.

punchline.text: Every piece of litter is a trap for something that can't read the label.

quiz.question: What percentage of seabirds now have plastic in their stomachs?

details.summary: Over 700 marine species are known to be harmed by plastic pollution through entanglement, ingestion, or habitat damage. Sea turtles mistake bags for jellyfish, seabirds feed plastic to their chicks, and whales have been found dead with stomachs full of plastic waste.
details.whyItMatters: Plastic is killing marine wildlife at industrial scale. The emotional and ecological impact drives public demand for action on plastic pollution and ocean conservation.
takeaways: Over 700 marine species are affected by plastic pollution
Ingestion and entanglement are the primary threats
Plastic enters marine food chains at every trophic level

faq.question: How many marine animals die from plastic each year?
faq.answer: Estimates suggest over 100,000 marine mammals and one million seabirds die annually from plastic ingestion or entanglement. The true number is likely much higher because most deaths go unobserved in the open ocean.

faq.question: How does plastic enter marine food chains?
faq.answer: Tiny organisms ingest microplastics, which are then consumed by small fish, and so on up the food chain. Toxins adsorbed onto plastic surfaces concentrate at each level. Humans eating seafood are at the top of this chain.
